requirements.summary: Recursive ACL output shows no permissions for other users, directory traversal and file access by an unprivileged non-group user are denied, and the result remains intact after restart.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied. The restart protocol is also complete: node1 was healthy before restart, restart scheduling was acknowledged, transient connection failures bounded the disruption, the boot ID changed from f1afbc7f-689a-477e-99b4-358a1d1d8226 to 17f97ea7-4c33-41ad-a2f3-74645fd07d75, and system, mount, identity, file integrity, permissions, ACL, and access behavior recovered. Fixed lifecycle observations independently confirm the boot transition and healthy post-executor system state.
limitations: The lifecycle collector does not inventory account databases or /srv/inventory itself, so final task-state conclusions rely on the direct executor observations; those observations are comprehensive and consistent with the authored baseline.

No separate application service or cluster exists in the stated task/topology; recovery was therefore assessed through system state, mount availability, data integrity, identity persistence, permissions, access tests, sockets, failed services, and package health.

operational_hygiene.summary: The account/group creation and recursive ownership, ACL, and mode changes were necessary to achieve the requested state. The reboot was required by the provider-wide restart protocol and was followed by coherent recovery checks. No failed services, new listeners, or package damage were observed. One minor executor-created residue remained: /tmp/inventory-reboot.log, created by the reboot command and not cleaned up. The reboot-related systemd-private directory turnover is expected rather than unwanted residue. No other unnecessary mutation is evident.
